lead: Multimedia is the use of a computer to present several kinds of media together — words, drawings, sound, moving pictures, animation — as one coordinated presentation. The computer controls what appears and when, and the user can often act on what is shown. That mix of many media, computer control and user action is what separates multimedia from a plain video clip. You meet it in railway enquiry kiosks, phone learning apps, hospital scan viewers and web advertisements. This chapter defines multimedia, lists its elements, and surveys where it is used.

sections.h3: Definition: many media under computer control

blocks.text: Multimedia means presenting information through several media at the same time, with a computer controlling what appears and when. A medium is a channel of information: words, a picture, a sound, a moving picture. Two media become multimedia only when a computer holds them together as one unit.

Three conditions must hold. First, at least two media types appear in the same presentation. Second, a computer, not a person changing slides, controls the order and the timing. Third, the media are integrated: the audio and the caption belong to the same scene, not to two unrelated files opened side by side.

When the presentation runs from start to end and the viewer only watches, it is linear multimedia. A cinema advertisement, or a health-awareness video looping on a hospital screen, is linear. When the viewer can decide what happens next — touch a button, click a train name, jump to a chapter — it is interactive multimedia. Interactivity is the feature examiners look for when the phrase is used.

Some syllabi call the elements 'media types'. Some also use hypermedia for interactive multimedia whose pieces are joined by links, as on a web page. The links are the extra idea; they are not a new media type.
Seven elements are usually listed. Each has its own digital unit, which Chapter 4.2 explains in full.

head: Element
What it carries
Typical example
rows: a train name on a kiosk
a route map drawn as lines
a touch button for the next page

blocks.text: Text is the cheapest element: a page of characters costs a few kilobytes. Graphics are stored as commands — draw this line, draw this curve — so a map stays sharp at any zoom. Images are stored as pixels and lose sharpness when enlarged. Unit 1, Graphics Systems and Output Primitives, covers this raster-versus-vector split.

Audio and video are timed media. Each carries a rate: audio samples per second, video frames per second. Animation is motion generated by the computer from key frames rather than captured by a camera. Interactivity is not a file at all; it is the program's response to a tap, a click, a key.

items: Education: a chemistry reaction shown as animation with a voice-over lets a student see the motion and hear the explanation at the same time, which a still page cannot do.
Entertainment: films with computer-generated effects, games, and streaming services that carry video, audio and subtitles together.
Advertising: a shop's web banner that plays a short clip and offers a 'Buy' button, so the message and the action sit in one place.
Medicine: a radiologist scrolls through CT slices as images, marks a region, and records a spoken note; telemedicine sends all three to a distant doctor.
Training: a flight simulator, or a repair module that shows a machine part in 3D and lets a technician rotate it.
Public information: a Chennai railway enquiry kiosk, a museum touch guide, or a bank branch screen that walks a customer through a form.

blocks.text: The common thread is control. The user picks a path instead of watching a fixed film. The price is size and bandwidth: a minute of video is thousands of times larger than a minute of text, which is why compression and codec hardware matter so much, and why the pieces must stay in step, the subject of Chapter 4.9. Full system design and delivery belong to Unit 6, Multimedia Systems and Applications.

examples.question: A Chennai railway enquiry kiosk shows a train name in text, a route map as graphics, a 20 s audio announcement, a 15 s video advertisement, a 2 s blinking icon as animation, and a touch button for the next page. (a) List the media elements present. (b) State why the kiosk is multimedia. (c) Find the total duration of the timed media in one play of the loop.
steps: Read the question and list every item named: train name, route map, 20 s announcement, 15 s advertisement, 2 s blinking icon, touch button.
Route map drawn as lines and curves is graphics.
The 20 s announcement is audio; its duration is 20 s.
The 15 s advertisement is video; its duration is 15 s.
The 2 s blinking icon, generated by the program, is animation; its duration is 2 s.
The touch button is interactivity. It is a control, not an information channel, so it has no duration.
Check computer control and integration: all items sit on one screen and are timed by the kiosk software, so the conditions hold. The user acts on the screen, so this is interactive multimedia.
Add the timed media: 20 s + 15 s + 2 s = 37 s.
examples.answer: The kiosk uses text, graphics, audio, video, animation and interactivity; the media are integrated under computer control and the user can act on them, so it is interactive multimedia, and one play of its timed media lasts 20 + 15 + 2 = 37 s.
examples.check:
audio_s = 20
video_s = 15
anim_s = 2
total_s = audio_s + video_s + anim_s
print(total_s)

examples.question: A 3-minute narration, a 45 s animation and one still diagram appear in an e-learning module. Which items are timed media, and what is the total timed duration in seconds?
steps: Convert the narration to seconds: 3 min × 60 s/min = 180 s.
The narration is audio, a timed medium: 180 s.
The animation is a timed medium: 45 s.
The still diagram is an image; it has no duration of its own, so it is not timed media.
Total timed duration = 180 s + 45 s = 225 s.
examples.answer: The narration and the animation are the timed media; together they last 180 + 45 = 225 s, that is 3 min 45 s.
examples.check:
narration_s = 3 * 60
anim_s = 45
total_s = narration_s + anim_s
print(narration_s)
print(total_s)

traps: A video clip alone is not multimedia. The examiner wants at least two media types plus computer control; interactivity is needed only when the phrase 'interactive multimedia' is used.
Do not list the keyboard, mouse or touch screen as media. They are input devices that support interactivity, not channels of information.
Text counts as a medium even though it feels ordinary. A slide with text and one photograph already carries two media.
Linear multimedia is still multimedia. Missing interactivity does not break the definition unless the question asks specifically for interactive multimedia.
Hypermedia is not a seventh element sitting beside audio and video. It is linked interactive multimedia, so do not add it to the element list.

quiz.a: Multimedia is the computer-controlled integration of two or more media types — such as text, graphics, audio, video and animation — into one presentation, often with user interaction.
Text, graphics, images, audio, video, animation and interactivity.

quiz.q: Why is a 30 s advertisement looping from a computer-controlled screen in a shop not interactive multimedia?
quiz.a: It is linear multimedia. A computer controls the order and timing, but the viewer has no control over what happens next; there is no input that changes the presentation.

quiz.q: Distinguish linear and interactive multimedia, giving one example of each.
quiz.a: In linear multimedia the presentation runs start to end with no user control, for example a health-awareness video on a hospital screen. In interactive multimedia the user decides the path, for example a railway kiosk where touching a train name opens its route map.

quiz.q: A museum touch guide plays a 40 s audio clip and a 25 s video about a painting, shows a 2 s rotating icon, and lets a visitor tap a painting to hear it. How many media types appear, and what is the total duration of the timed media?
quiz.a: Media types: audio, video, animation and interactivity, so four. The audio and video are timed, plus the 2 s animation loop: 40 + 25 + 2 = 67 s of timed media.

quiz.q: A module contains a 2-minute narration, a 30 s animation, a 10 s video and a still diagram. Find the total timed duration in seconds and in minutes.
quiz.a: Narration = 2 × 60 = 120 s. The diagram is not timed. Total = 120 + 30 + 10 = 160 s, which is 160 ÷ 60 ≈ 2 min 40 s.

quiz.q: A kiosk plays a video with sound but ignores every touch on its screen. Is it interactive multimedia? State what single change would make it so.
quiz.a: No. With video and audio only, it is linear multimedia; the plays run start to end. The change is to make the software respond to a touch, for example a button that pauses the video or opens a route map, which adds interactivity.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry the same definition scales up to streaming platforms, where one film arrives as compressed video, several audio tracks and subtitle streams, held together by synchronization metadata. Authoring has moved to the browser, where video elements, canvas drawing and WebGL supply the media and JavaScript supplies the interactivity. Search for 'hypermedia' and 'multimedia authoring' to go further.
